collection.name: HoldsUp prototype collection
collection.scope: 21 well-known psychology findings, each paired with at least one large replication, multi-lab study or meta-analysis. Hand-curated for a coursework prototype; not a complete record.

findings.name: Ego depletion
findings.claim: Exerting self-control on one task leaves people with less self-control for the next task.
findings.status_note: Two large preregistered multi-lab studies found an effect close to zero.

original.title: Ego depletion: Is the active self a limited resource?
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1252–1265

replications.title: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect
replications.summary: 23 labs (N = 2,141) ran a standard sequential-task protocol; the pooled effect was small, with a confidence interval that included zero.

replications.title: A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect
replications.summary: 36 labs (N = 3,531); the preregistered analyses did not find evidence for a depletion effect.

findings.name: Facial feedback hypothesis
findings.claim: Making a facial expression, such as a smile, changes how strongly people feel the matching emotion.
findings.status_note: The classic pen-in-mouth study failed a 17-lab replication, but a 2022 adversarial collaboration found small effects for posed smiles.

original.title: Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(5), 768–777

replications.authors: Wagenmakers, Beek, Dijkhoff, Gronau et al.
replications.title: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988)
replications.summary: 17 labs; the original rating difference of 0.82 points shrank to 0.03, with a confidence interval spanning zero.

replications.authors: Coles, March, Marmolejo-Ramos et al. (Many Smiles Collaboration)
replications.title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration
replications.summary: Mimicking or voluntarily posing a smile increased reported happiness; the pen-in-mouth version was less conclusive.

findings.name: Power posing
findings.claim: Holding an expansive 'power pose' for a minute or two raises testosterone, lowers cortisol and increases risk-taking.
findings.status_note: Larger studies found no effect on hormones or risk-taking; the effect on self-reported feelings of power did hold.

original.title: Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance

replications.authors: Ranehill, Dreber, Johannesson, Leiberg, Sul & Weber
replications.title: Assessing the robustness of power posing
replications.summary: With N = 200, power posing raised self-reported feelings of power but did not change hormone levels or risk-taking.

findings.contested: One of the original authors (Carney) later said publicly that she no longer believes the effect is real.

findings.name: Elderly priming (walking speed)
findings.claim: Unscrambling words linked to old age makes people walk more slowly afterwards, without their awareness.
findings.status_note: A replication with automated timing found no effect, except when experimenters expected slow walking.

original.title: Automaticity of social behavior: Direct effects of trait construct and stereotype activation on action
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 71(2), 230–244

replications.title: Behavioral priming: It's all in the mind, but whose mind?
replications.summary: Infrared timing showed no slowing; a slowing effect appeared only when experimenters were led to expect it.

findings.contested: The original author disputed the replication's procedure.

findings.name: Professor priming (intelligence priming)
findings.claim: Thinking about professors, rather than football hooligans, improves performance on a general-knowledge quiz.
findings.status_note: A 40-lab registered replication found essentially no difference between conditions.

original.title: The relation between perception and behavior, or how to win a game of Trivial Pursuit
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(4), 865–877

replications.title: Registered Replication Report: Dijksterhuis and van Knippenberg (1998)
replications.summary: The original reported a 13.1% advantage; the multi-lab estimate was about 0.1%.

findings.name: Money (currency) priming
aliases: money makes people endorse the system
findings.claim: Brief exposure to images of money increases endorsement of free-market and system-justifying beliefs.
findings.status_note: Did not replicate in Many Labs 1 or in four high-powered direct replications.

original.title: Mere exposure to money increases endorsement of free-market systems and social inequality

replications.title: Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project
replications.summary: One of two effects (with flag priming) out of 13 that did not replicate across 36 samples (N = 6,344).

replications.title: Do subtle reminders of money change people's political views?
replications.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(4), e73–e85
replications.summary: High-powered replications of four money-priming effects found no evidence of priming (weighted d = 0.03).

findings.name: Flag priming
findings.claim: A brief glimpse of the American flag shifts people's political attitudes towards conservatism.
findings.status_note: Did not replicate across 36 samples in Many Labs 1.

original.title: A single exposure to the American flag shifts support toward Republicanism up to 8 months later

replications.title: Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project
replications.summary: Did not replicate; the one significant sample effect ran in the wrong direction.

findings.name: Anchoring effect
findings.claim: An arbitrary number shown first pulls later numerical estimates towards it.
findings.status_note: Replicated across 36 samples in Many Labs 1, with effects larger than originally reported.

original.title: Measures of anchoring in estimation tasks

replications.title: Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project
replications.summary: Replicated consistently; anchoring was stronger than in the original study.

findings.name: Gain–loss framing (Asian disease problem)
findings.claim: People choose the safe option when outcomes are described as gains, and the risky option when the same outcomes are described as losses.
findings.status_note: Replicated in both Many Labs 1 and Many Labs 2.

original.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice

replications.title: Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project
replications.summary: Replicated consistently across 36 samples.

replications.title: Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings
replications.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443–490
replications.summary: Replicated in a much larger multi-country sample.

findings.name: Sunk cost effect
findings.claim: People are more likely to continue with something they have already paid for, even when the past cost should not matter.
findings.status_note: The version tested in Many Labs 1 replicated consistently.

original.title: Instructional manipulation checks: Detecting satisficing to increase statistical power

replications.title: Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project
replications.summary: Among the 10 of 13 effects that replicated consistently.

findings.name: Cleanliness and moral judgement
findings.claim: Feeling physically clean makes people judge moral wrongdoing less harshly.
findings.status_note: A direct replication with over 0.99 power found no effect; the original author disputes the replication.

original.title: With a clean conscience: Cleanliness reduces the severity of moral judgments

replications.title: Does cleanliness influence moral judgments? A direct replication of Schnall, Benton, and Harvey (2008)
replications.summary: No evidence that cleanliness reduced the severity of moral judgements.

findings.contested: The original author argued that a ceiling effect in the replication data explains the difference.

findings.name: Physical warmth and interpersonal warmth
findings.claim: Holding something warm makes people judge others as warmer and act more generously.
findings.status_note: Several high-powered replications found near-zero effects.

original.title: Experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth

replications.authors: Lynott, Corker, Wortman, Connell, Donnellan, Lucas & O'Brien
replications.title: Replication of 'Experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth' by Williams & Bargh (2008)
replications.summary: Three labs found no effect, separately or combined.

replications.title: No evidence that experiencing physical warmth promotes interpersonal warmth: Two failures to replicate Williams and Bargh (2008)
replications.summary: Both experiments, with about three times the original samples, found near-zero effects.

findings.name: Marshmallow test (delay of gratification predicts later success)
findings.claim: How long a preschool child waits for a larger reward strongly predicts their later academic and social outcomes.
findings.status_note: The link exists but is about half the originally reported size, and shrinks by about two thirds after controlling for family background.

original.title: Predicting adolescent cognitive and self-regulatory competencies from preschool delay of gratification

replications.title: Revisiting the marshmallow test: A conceptual replication investigating links between early delay of gratification and later outcomes
replications.summary: In about 900 children, the correlation was half the original size and fell sharply with controls.

findings.name: Verbal overshadowing
findings.claim: Describing a face in words makes people worse at recognising it later.
findings.status_note: A large registered replication found a robust effect, smaller than the original and dependent on timing.

original.title: Verbal overshadowing of visual memories: Some things are better left unsaid

replications.title: Registered Replication Report: Schooler and Engstler-Schooler (1990)
replications.summary: Describers were 4% to 16% less likely to pick the right person, depending on when the description was given.

findings.name: Precognition (Bem's 'Feeling the future')
findings.claim: Studying words after a memory test improves recall of those words on the earlier test.
findings.status_note: Three preregistered exact replications found no effect.

original.title: Feeling the future: Experimental evidence for anomalous retroactive influences on cognition and affect
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 100(3), 407–425

replications.title: Failing the future: Three unsuccessful attempts to replicate Bem's 'retroactive facilitation of recall' effect
replications.summary: All three attempts (combined n = 150) found no significant effect.

findings.name: Unconscious thought advantage
findings.claim: For complex choices, people decide better after being distracted than after deliberating consciously.
findings.status_note: A meta-analysis and a large replication (N = 399) found no reliable advantage.

original.title: On making the right choice: The deliberation-without-attention effect

replications.authors: Nieuwenstein, Wierenga, Morey, Wicherts, Blom, Wagenmakers & van Rijn
replications.title: On making the right choice: A meta-analysis and large-scale replication attempt of the unconscious thought advantage
replications.summary: Concluded there is no reliable support for the claim.

findings.name: Choice overload (jam study)
findings.claim: Offering many options instead of a few makes people less likely to choose at all and less satisfied when they do.
findings.status_note: A meta-analysis of 50 experiments found an average effect near zero, with large variation between studies.

original.title: When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing?
original.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006

replications.title: Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload
replications.summary: Mean effect virtually zero across 63 conditions (N = 5,036), but with considerable variance, suggesting it holds only under some conditions.

findings.name: Obedience to authority (Milgram)
findings.claim: Most people will continue giving what they believe are painful shocks when instructed by an authority figure.
findings.status_note: A partial replication stopping at 150 volts found obedience rates only slightly lower than Milgram's.

original.title: Behavioral study of obedience
original.venue: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4), 371–378

replications.title: Replicating Milgram: Would people still obey today?
replications.summary: 70% continued past 150 volts, against 82.5% in the matching Milgram condition; the difference was not significant.

findings.contested: This was a partial replication: for ethical reasons it stopped at 150 volts rather than 450.

findings.name: Stereotype threat (women and mathematics)
findings.claim: Reminding women of the stereotype that women are worse at maths lowers their maths test performance.
findings.status_note: A large registered replication in Dutch schools found no effect; earlier meta-analyses had reported smaller, bias-sensitive effects.

original.title: Stereotype threat and women's math performance

replications.title: The influence of gender stereotype threat on mathematics test scores of Dutch high school students: A registered report
replications.summary: With N = 2,064 students, found no overall or moderated stereotype-threat effect among girls.

findings.contested: The replication's authors note the result may not generalise beyond Dutch 13–14 year-olds.

findings.name: Mozart effect
aliases: listening to Mozart makes you smarter
findings.claim: Listening to a Mozart sonata briefly improves spatial reasoning performance.
findings.status_note: Brief improvements appear, but about as large after other music; a meta-analysis of about 40 studies found little evidence for a Mozart-specific effect.

original.title: Music and spatial task performance

replications.title: Mozart effect–Shmozart effect: A meta-analysis
replications.summary: Small effect compared with silence, a similar effect for other music, and larger effects in studies by the original group.

findings.contested: Sources differ: FLoRA records a successful replication of the original study, while the meta-analysis concludes there is no specific Mozart effect.

findings.name: Stroop effect
findings.claim: People are slower to name the ink colour of a word when the word spells a different colour.
findings.status_note: One of the most reliably reproduced effects in psychology; a 1991 review covered half a century of replications.

original.title: Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions

replications.title: Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review
replications.summary: Integrative review of decades of studies reproducing the interference effect.
